statement: Jo picks a whole number from $1$ to $20$, and Sam picks a whole number from $1$ to $15$. Of all the possible pairs of picks, for how many is the product of the two numbers even?

choices.misconception: I added the $10$ even numbers Jo could pick and the $7$ even numbers Sam could pick, getting $17$, instead of counting pairs.
I counted the pairs with an odd product, $10 \cdot 8 = 80$, instead of the pairs with an even product.
I thought exactly half of the $20 \cdot 15 = 300$ pairs give an even product.
I added the $10 \cdot 15 = 150$ pairs where Jo's number is even and the $20 \cdot 7 = 140$ pairs where Sam's number is even, counting the pairs where both are even twice.

hints: A product of two whole numbers is odd only when both numbers are odd.
Count the pairs with an odd product, then subtract from the total number of pairs.
There are $20 \cdot 15 = 300$ pairs. Jo has $10$ odd numbers to choose from and Sam has $8$.

solutions.reliable: There are $20 \cdot 15 = 300$ pairs. A product is odd exactly when both numbers are odd. Jo has $10$ odd choices ($1, 3, \ldots, 19$) and Sam has $8$ ($1, 3, \ldots, 15$), so $10 \cdot 8 = 80$ pairs have an odd product. The other $300 - 80 = 220$ pairs have an even product.
solutions.elegant: Sort by Jo's pick. If Jo's number is even ($10$ ways), every one of Sam's $15$ numbers gives an even product: $150$ pairs. If Jo's number is odd ($10$ ways), Sam's number must be even ($7$ ways): $70$ pairs. The total is $150 + 70 = 220$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
